# Volume 5 — CHAPTER XXIX. A WEIRD TALE

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

During an evening in early June, Fern Hollow proved to be a thoroughly enchanting spot, a fact the children recognized as they were seated in the unshaded glade where the bells produced an elfin ring on the Tree Lovers, and the green tresses of the White Lady swayed. Like a faithful, joyful companion, the wind laughed and whistled around them. A spicy fragrance rose from the young ferns in the hollow. Scattered across the valley amidst the dark firs, the wild cherry trees appeared mistily white. Over in the maples behind Hollowmere, the robins were whistling. Further off, upon the Glen's slopes, fruit-laden orchards bloomed in the dusk's veil, looking sweet, mystic, and wonderful. It was springtime, a season when youth is meant to be joyful. Everyone in Fern Hollow felt that joy that evening—up to the moment when Mary Stubbs chilled them to the bone by recounting the tale of Henry Warren’s ghost.
{: #nw-v05-c29-p0000 }

Kit was absent. Kit passed his evenings these days preparing for his entrance examination in the Hollowmere garret. Tobias was by the pond, fishing for trout. Edmund had read Longfellow’s sea poems to the rest of them, and they were filled with the beauty and mystery of the ships. Afterwards, they discussed what they would accomplish once they grew up—the places they would travel to—the distant, lovely shores they would behold. Bess and Izzy intended to travel to Europe. Edmund desired the Nile lamenting past its Egyptian sands, alongside a sight of the sphinx. Grace suggested somewhat gloomily that she imagined she would be forced to become a missionary—old Mrs. Taylor informed her she should be one—and in that way she would at least view India or China, those mysterious lands of the Orient. Rupert’s heart was determined on African jungles. Ida remained silent. She believed she would simply prefer to remain at home. This place was more beautiful than any other. It would be terrible when they had all grown up and were forced to disperse across the globe. The mere thought made Ida experience loneliness and homesickness. However, the others continued dreaming joyfully until Mary Stubbs showed up and dispelled poetry and dreams all at once.
{: #nw-v05-c29-p0001 }

“My goodness, I have lost my breath,” she cried out. “I hurried down the slope at top speed. Something gave me a terrible fright up at the former Bailey property.”
{: #nw-v05-c29-p0002 }

“What gave you a fright?” Izzy inquired.
{: #nw-v05-c29-p0003 }

“I’m not sure. I was searching beneath those lilacs in the former garden, attempting to check whether any lilies-of-the-valley had emerged so far. That spot was pitch black—and unexpectedly I noticed a moving and whispering noise on the far side of the garden, among those cherry bushes. A white thing was there. I assure you that I didn’t delay to look again. I rushed across the dyke as fast as possible. I felt certain that Henry Warren’s ghost was there.”
{: #nw-v05-c29-p0004 }

“Henry Warren was who?” Izzy inquired.
{: #nw-v05-c29-p0005 }

“And for what reason ought he to possess a phantom?” Bess inquired.
{: #nw-v05-c29-p0006 }

“Laws, were you never told the tale? And you raised in the Glen. Well, hold on a moment until I regain my full breath and I will inform you.”
{: #nw-v05-c29-p0007 }

Edmund felt a delightful shiver run through him. Ghost stories were something he adored. He derived a frightening, wonderful enjoyment from their strangeness, their tense endings, and their uncanny nature. Longfellow lost all its appeal and became mundane at once. Tossing the volume to the side, he extended his body, leaning up on his elbows so he could give his full attention, and trained his large, glowing eyes directly on Mary’s face. Mary preferred that he not stare at her in that manner. It seemed to her that she would perform the ghost story more effectively if Edmund’s gaze was turned away. She would be able to include various embellishments and make up some creative elements to heighten the terror. Given the circumstances, however, she was forced to adhere strictly to the plain truth—or to what she had received as the truth.
{: #nw-v05-c29-p0008 }

“Well,” she commenced, “you are aware that ancient Tom Bailey and his spouse resided in that dwelling up there three decades back. He was a terrible old scoundrel, according to rumor, and his spouse was not much superior. They possessed no offspring of their own, but a sibling of old Tom passed away and left behind a young lad—this Henry Warren—and they accepted him. He was roughly twelve upon his arrival to them, and somewhat small and frail. People claim Tom and his spouse treated him terribly from the beginning—lashed him and deprived him of food. People remarked they desired his death so that they might obtain the modest sum of money his mother had bequeathed to him. Henry did not perish immediately, but he commenced having seizures—epileps, as they termed them—and he developed into a somewhat simple youth, until he reached roughly eighteen. His uncle was accustomed to beating him in that garden up there because it was situated behind the dwelling where nobody could observe him. Nevertheless people could listen, and they claim it was terrible on occasion listening to poor Henry beg his uncle not to slay him. Yet no one ventured to intervene because old Tom was such a villain he would certainly have retaliated against them in some fashion. He set fire to the barns of an individual at Harbour Head who angered him. Finally Henry passed away and his uncle and aunt announced he perished during one of his seizures and that was everything anyone ever learned, yet everyone asserted Tom had simply up and murdered him permanently in the end. And before long word spread that Henry walked. That ancient garden was haunted. He was detected there during evenings, groaning and weeping. Old Tom and his spouse departed—relocated out West and never returned. The property acquired such an ill reputation no person would purchase or lease it. That is the reason it has completely fallen into decay. That occurred three decades back, yet Henry Warren’s spirit haunts it still.”
{: #nw-v05-c29-p0009 }

“Is that something you believe?” Bess inquired with disdain. “It’s not something I do.”
{: #nw-v05-c29-p0010 }

“Well, decent folk have observed him—and listened to him,” Mary answered back. “They claim he shows himself and crawls on the dirt and grips you around the legs and jabbers and laments the way he used to when he lived. I remembered that the moment I spotted that pale object in the shrubs and figured if it seized me in that manner and lamented I’d fall down dead right there. Therefore I bolted and fled. It may not have been his phantom, but I didn't intend to risk anything with a spectre.”
{: #nw-v05-c29-p0011 }

“Old Mrs. Stimson’s white calf was probably what it was,” Izzy laughed. “That garden is where it grazes—I’ve noticed it there.”
{: #nw-v05-c29-p0012 }

“That could be true. However, I will no longer take the path through the Bailey garden to go home. Tobias has arrived carrying a large catch of trout, and the responsibility to cook them now falls on me. According to both Kit and Tobias, my cooking surpasses everyone else's in the Glen. Additionally, Winifred permitted me to carry this collection of cookies up here. I nearly spilled them the moment I spotted Henry’s ghost.”
{: #nw-v05-c29-p0013 }

Tobias let out a hoot upon hearing the tale of the ghost—a story Mary iterated while she cooked the fish, embellishing it slightly, given that Edmund had left to assist Grace with laying the table. Tobias remained entirely unaffected by it, yet Grace, Ida, and Rupert were inwardly terrified, even if they refused to admit as much. Everything was fine while the rest of the group accompanied them in the valley; however, once the meal concluded and darkness began to descend, the memory made them tremble. Tobias ascended to Hollowmere alongside the Carrows to consult Kit regarding a matter, and Mary Stubbs took that route on her journey back. Consequently, Grace, Ida, and Rupert were forced to return to the manse by themselves. Walking in tight formation, they steered well clear of the old Bailey garden. Naturally, they didn't think it was haunted, but they refused to approach it nonetheless.
{: #nw-v05-c29-p0014 }
